# Opal Pettigrew

## Overview

- **Gender:** female  <sub>[v1 c35 P1](../source/v01-c35.md#nw-v01-c35-p0001), [v3 c14 P5](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0005)</sub>
- **Status:** deceased  <sub>[v3 c14 P30](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0030)</sub>
- **Origin:** Brierley  <sub>[v1 c35 P0](../source/v01-c35.md#nw-v01-c35-p0000), [v3 c14 P30](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0030)</sub>
- **Role:** schoolteacher  <sub>[v3 c14 P2](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0002)</sub>

## Appearance

Opal was widely considered the most beautiful girl in her school and community, possessing striking features, a radiant complexion, big vivid blue eyes, and a full, eye-catching figure. She was especially noted for her gorgeous, long yellow hair braids, which she wore long when in town. During her fatal illness, her complexion grew pale with a hectic flush and she appeared thin and childlike. In death, her features were so hallowed and delicate that she was remembered as the most beautiful deceased person seen in Brierley.

_Sources: [v1 c30 P43](../source/v01-c30.md#nw-v01-c30-p0043), [v1 c35 P1](../source/v01-c35.md#nw-v01-c35-p0001), [v1 c35 P6](../source/v01-c35.md#nw-v01-c35-p0006), [v3 c14 P5](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0005), [v3 c14 P31](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0031), [v4 c12 P15](../source/v04-c12.md#nw-v04-c12-p0015)_

## Personality

In her youth, Opal maintained a perpetually cheerful, sunny, and pleasant disposition, openly enjoying life's pleasures and engaging in frequent laughter. She possessed a somewhat superficial and worldly nature, lacking interest in deep literature or intellectual conversations. She delighted in boasting about her numerous suitors, drives, parties, and dresses. Beneath her merry exterior, however, she harbored a deep vulnerability and terror of death and the unfamiliarity of the afterlife, ultimately showing gratitude and affection for true friendship in her final days.

_Sources: [v1 c35 P1](../source/v01-c35.md#nw-v01-c35-p0001), [v1 c35 P3](../source/v01-c35.md#nw-v01-c35-p0003), [v3 c14 P2](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0002), [v3 c14 P11](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0011), [v3 c14 P13](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0013), [v3 c14 P23](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0023), [v3 c14 P27](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0027), [v3 c14 P31](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0031)_

## History

Opal grew up in Brierley as one of several daughters in the Pettigrew family. As a young student, she participated in local games, such as an attempt to dramatize Tennyson's Arthurian poetry at Pembroke's pond, though she declined to play Elaine due to her fear of acting deceased. While attending Regent's Academy, she was recognized as the most beautiful girl in her class and frequently walked home from the train accompanied by Hugh Carrow. She later took up a position as a teacher at Pale Sands school. However, her health began to fail rapidly, forcing her to step down until the new year. Throughout her final summer, she suffered from a consuming illness—likely consumption—and spent many smoky afternoons in her family's garden resting in a hammock. Realizing her approaching end, she confided her terror of death and the unfamiliarity of heaven to Nell Harcourt. She passed away peacefully in her sleep the morning after a village party, leaving an unfinished piece of needlework to Nell. She was laid to rest in the ancient cemetery near the Brierley church.

_Sources: [v1 c28 P1](../source/v01-c28.md#nw-v01-c28-p0001), [v1 c35 P0](../source/v01-c35.md#nw-v01-c35-p0000), [v1 c35 P1](../source/v01-c35.md#nw-v01-c35-p0001), [v1 c35 P6](../source/v01-c35.md#nw-v01-c35-p0006), [v3 c14 P0](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0000), [v3 c14 P2](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0002), [v3 c14 P5](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0005), [v3 c14 P6](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0006), [v3 c14 P7](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0007), [v3 c14 P11](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0011), [v3 c14 P13](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0013), [v3 c14 P30](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0030), [v3 c14 P33](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0033)_

## Quotes

> Floating downward does not bother me when two or three of us are occupying the flat and we are able to sit upright. During those times, it is enjoyable. However, lying flat and acting as if I were deceased—that is something I simply could not do. Fear would actually kill me.  <sub>[v1 c28 P1](../source/v01-c28.md#nw-v01-c28-p0001)</sub>

> The cemetery appears so peculiar under the moon’s light! So spectral! Nell, the time is drawing near when I will be resting in that place. You, Isolde, and everyone else will be moving around, brimming with vitality—while I will be situated there—within the ancient cemetery—deceased!  <sub>[v3 c14 P7](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0007)</sub>

> Because—because—oh, Nell, I am not scared that I will fail to get into heaven. I belong to the church. But—everything there is going to be so unfamiliar. I ponder—and ponder—and it makes me so scared—and—and—homesick. Of course, heaven has to be extremely beautiful, as the Bible states—however, Nell, it will not be like what I am accustomed to.  <sub>[v3 c14 P13](../source/v03-c14.md#nw-v03-c14-p0013)</sub>
